title: Why, and how you need to sandbox AI-Generated Code? — Harshil Agrawal, Cloudflare

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

Security and defense is the core subject, with implementations built on Cloudflare's developer platform. Content spans architectural design of isolation boundaries, deployment of sandboxed execution environments, and operational security practices. Requires JavaScript and web architecture familiarity but remains accessible to working developers. Conference talk with live code demonstrations and architecture walkthroughs. summary: Harshil Agrawal frames AI-generated code as untrusted code from the internet, noting that LLMs produce text that looks like code—sometimes correct, sometimes subtly wrong, and sometimes dangerous through hallucination, over-helpfulness, or adversarial prompt injection (direct and indirect). The core danger is that AI-generated code runs with the application's full production privileges—file system, environment variables, network, database, and API keys. He advocates capability-based security: default-deny everything, then explicitly grant minimal capabilities, mirroring browsers and mobile operating systems. He presents an isolation spectrum: eval (never for untrusted code), V8 isolates (lightweight, sub-millisecond startup, no file system), and containers (full Linux environment, seconds to start, heavier resources). He defines a five-part threat model: secrets, networking, file system access, multi-tenant isolation, and resource exhaustion. He demonstrates two applications. The first, an OpenClaw alternative, uses Cloudflare dynamic worker isolates for fast JavaScript skill execution. The isolate architecture sets globalOutbound to null (blocking all network), passes only explicitly granted bindings—a restricted database interface and a logger—and routes calls through worker RPC. Network access has three options: null (fully blocked, recommended), proxied through your service (allow-list, logging, rate limits), or fully open (never recommended). The second application, Prompt Motion (promptmotion.app), generates videos from user descriptions and requires containers because it needs git clone, npm install, dev servers, and port exposure. Each user gets their own container; the architecture uses a worker calling a Sandbox SDK managed by a durable object. Critical patterns include: never share sandboxes between users, never pass API keys into sandboxes (use a proxy pattern), and always clean up containers using try-finally with maximum lifetime timeouts. He then extends the decision tree with concrete examples—code interpreters and data transformation pipelines use isolates; building applications and running test suites use containers—and notes that in practice both are used together: isolates as the fast brain for tool-calling loops, containers as the workbench for building real things. He closes with a universal eight-item checklist applicable to any sandboxing technology: default-deny network access, grant explicit capabilities, isolate per user, set resource limits, keep secrets outside the sandbox, clean up sandboxes, log everything for audit trails, and validate input before execution. He emphasizes that AI-generated code is functionally equivalent to code from an anonymous contributor and must be sandboxed, constrained, and verified every time. Resources include dynamicworkers.com documentation for isolates, the sandbox SDK documentation for containers, and code mode as an AI agent integration pattern.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: AI-generated code is untrusted code from the internet—equivalent to running a random code snippet found online in production—and must be sandboxed, constrained, and verified every single time.
Capability-based security means default-deny everything, then explicitly grant minimal capabilities; enumerate what to allow, not what to block.
In practice you will use both isolates and containers together: isolates as the fast brain for rapid tool-calling iterations, containers as the workbench for building and deploying real applications.
V8 isolates provide strong isolation with minimal code: set globalOutbound to null, pass only explicitly granted bindings—dangerous operations are never available, not intercepted.
Each user gets their own sandbox; the user ID is the isolation boundary. Never share sandboxes—the cost of an extra sandbox is always less than the cost of a data leak.
Never pass API keys into sandboxes. Use the proxy pattern: the sandbox calls your worker's endpoint, the worker adds authentication and forwards the request.
Always clean up containers using try-finally with maximum lifetime timeouts. Idle sandboxes cost money and are a security surface.

Apply a universal eight-item checklist regardless of technology: default-deny network, explicit capabilities, one sandbox per user, resource limits, secrets outside sandbox, cleanup, logging, and input validation.
Decision tree: if code needs a file system, processes, or package installs, use containers; otherwise use isolates (faster, cheaper, simpler, tighter isolation).
Identify and articulate the security risks of running AI-generated code with full application privileges.

sections.title: The Problem: AI-Generated Code as Untrusted Code
sections.summary: Harshil introduces the core problem: LLM-generated code is effectively untrusted code from the internet. He traces the evolution from autocomplete to autonomous agents and frames three threat scenarios—hallucination, over-helpful LLMs reading secrets, and prompt injection (direct and indirect)—emphasizing that AI code runs with full production privileges.

sections.title: Capability-Based Security as the Solution
sections.summary: He presents capability-based security as the unifying principle behind browsers, operating systems, and mobile platforms: default-deny everything, then explicitly grant minimal capabilities. This allow-list approach contrasts with block-list approaches that must enumerate every possible attack.

sections.title: Isolation Spectrum and Threat Model
sections.summary: He outlines the isolation spectrum from eval (zero isolation, never use) through V8 isolates (lightweight, sub-millisecond, no file system) to containers (full Linux, seconds to start). He defines a concrete five-part threat model: secrets, networking, file system access, multi-tenant isolation, and resource exhaustion.

sections.title: Two Real Applications and Isolate Architecture
sections.summary: He introduces two applications with different sandboxing needs: an OpenClaw alternative using V8 isolates for fast JavaScript skill execution, and a motion graphics app using containers for full file systems and processes. He demonstrates the first app and explains the dynamic worker isolate architecture.

sections.title: Isolate Architecture Deep Dive and Network Control
sections.summary: He walks through the isolate code: globalOutbound null blocks all network, only explicitly granted bindings are available. He explains the network control spectrum—null (recommended), proxied (allow-list), or fully open (never for untrusted code)—and honestly covers isolate trade-offs as features for short-lived tool calls.

sections.title: Container Architecture: Prompt Motion App
sections.summary: He demonstrates Prompt Motion, a video generator app requiring git clone, npm install, dev servers, and port exposure. Each user gets their own container with isolated file systems. The architecture uses a worker calling a Sandbox SDK managed by a durable object orchestrating container VMs.

sections.title: Critical Container Patterns: Isolation, Secrets, Cleanup
sections.summary: He details three critical patterns: one user per sandbox, the proxy pattern for secrets (never pass API keys into sandboxes), and container cleanup using try-finally with maximum lifetime timeouts. Cloudflare containers default to 10-minute timeouts.

sections.title: Decision Tree: Isolates vs Containers
sections.summary: He provides a decision tree: if code needs a file system, processes, or package installs, use containers; otherwise use isolates. Most AI agent tool calling and code interpreters fit the isolate use case.

sections.title: Combining Approaches and Universal Checklist
sections.summary: He extends the decision tree with concrete examples and notes that in practice both approaches are used together: isolates as the fast brain for rapid tool-calling iterations, containers as the workbench for building real things. He presents a universal eight-item checklist applicable to any sandboxing technology: default-deny network, explicit capabilities, one sandbox per user, resource limits, secrets outside sandbox, cleanup, logging for audit trails, and input validation. He closes by reiterating that AI-generated code is untrusted code—functionally equivalent to code from an anonymous contributor—and must be sandboxed, constrained, and verified every time. He recaps four main topics and shares resources including dynamicworkers.com, sandbox SDK docs, and code mode.

demonstrations: OpenClaw alternative built on Cloudflare's developer platform using dynamic worker isolates to execute AI-generated JavaScript skills on the fly, demonstrated by asking the agent to fetch top stories from Hacker News.

Prompt Motion (promptmotion.app), a live production video generator app where AI writes motion code, clones a starter repository, installs NPM dependencies, starts a dev server, and exposes a preview URL using containers, demonstrated by adding a highlight on a user-provided logo.
limitations: V8 isolates lack a file system and process model, making them unsuitable for use cases requiring npm install, dev servers, or repository cloning.
Isolates only run JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, or WebAssembly—no arbitrary binaries, Go, Rust, or compiled code.
Isolates are stateless; each invocation is a fresh context requiring externalized state.
Isolates have resource limits on CPU time and memory, unsuitable for heavy compute workloads.
Containers are more expensive, slower to start (seconds vs milliseconds), and architecturally more complex with more moving parts.
Block-list approaches require enumerating every possible attack scenario and missing one leads to compromise.
quantitativeClaims: V8 isolates start in a quarter millisecond.
Containers take a few seconds to start.
AI code generation evolved from autocomplete to autonomous agents in approximately 2 years.
Cloudflare containers have a default timeout of 10 minutes.
Following all eight checklist items puts you in a fundamentally better position than 95% of AI applications running code today.
